results.title: Proper way to calculate inter-annotator agreement for ...
results.content: Published Time: 2022-06-29T20:12:28+00:00 Proper way to calculate inter-annotator agreement for spans/ner? Proper way to calculate inter-annotator agreement for spans/ner? How would I go about computing a inter-annotator agreement score for a ner task where the annotators may have different number of annotations per documents? Some ideas I was thinking about: find only the annotations that have overlap, then calculate absolute span matching (if they are the exact same span), percent overlap, and levenshtein distance. Any help would be greatly appreciated 5.7k views 6 likes 7 links A couple of initial questions. * How many annotators will you have (a few like 2-3 or many 5+)? And will they all review the same ones or will each see different ones (e.g., every item is reviewed by three annotators but each annotator sees different examples)? * When you say overlap, I assume you mean the union of all annotated spans (e.g., all spans that had at least 1 annotator)? I ask b/c these could factor in a difference in performance (e.g., very technical text with expert annotators may have a lot of overlap as shared knowledge of entities while open-ended tasks to non-experts may have very little overlap in spans). How would I go about computing a inter-annotator agreement score for a ner task where the annotators may have different number of annotations per documents? Grouin et al., 2011 also may help as they calculate Kappa, Scott's Pi or F-Measure but on a subset of terms with at least one annotator (e.g., pooling/span-overlap), only n-grams or noun-phrases only. Wang et al., 2021 had a variety of different ways to calculate overlap (quoted from supplemental materials): * Exact span matches, where two annotators identified exact the same Named Entity text spans. * Relaxed span matches, where Named Entity text spans from two annotators overlap. * Exact concept matches, where within agreed text span, annotators assigned exact same concept class. * Parent concept matches, where the concept class assigned by one annotator is the parent class of the one by the other annotator. * Ambiguity concept matches, where one annotator assigned a semantic ambiguous class which includes the concept assigned by the other annotator.

results.title: How Database Triggers and Stored Procedures Automate Business Logic
results.content: Published Time: 2025-02-26 How Database Triggers and Stored Procedures Automate Business Logic - Database Management How Database Triggers and Stored Procedures Automate Business Logic How Database Triggers and Stored Procedures Automate Business Logic Unlocking the full potential of database systems often hinges on automating critical tasks. Database triggers and stored procedures stand as silent sentinels, ensuring data integrity and enforcing business logic seamlessly. * Respond to Changes in Real-Time ### Leverage Technology for Innovation As someone who has always been deeply interested in leveraging technology for innovation, I've had the opportunity to work on numerous projects where database triggers and stored procedures played an essential role in automating data validation and business logic. I employed database triggers and stored procedures to automate data validation and streamline complex business logic for multi-currency transactions. In summary, combining triggers and stored procedures provided a robust framework for consistent data validation and centralized business logic. Stored procedures can also aid in preserving data integrity by executing complex routines that ensure business logic is consistently applied. By automating these tasks, both triggers and stored procedures streamline data handling processes, ensuring efficient and consistent execution of business logic. ### Automate Data Management Through the automated responses of triggers to data changes and the on-demand execution of stored procedures, businesses can greatly reduce the need for manual data management. To maximize these benefits, businesses should incorporate triggers and stored procedures into their database management practices. ### Enforce Business Rules Automatically Database triggers act immediately when specific data changes occur, ensuring that essential business rules are automatically enforced without requiring manual intervention. Stored procedures, meanwhile, can execute complex logic and operations whenever called upon, ensuring that the same standards and rules are consistently applied across various operations. This not only simplifies the data management process but also ensures a higher degree of accuracy and reliability in business operations. ### Respond to Changes in Real-Time By leveraging database triggers, organizations can automatically respond to changes and perform necessary adjustments in real-time, ensuring that all data remains consistent. Stored procedures, which can be executed as needed, allow for the encapsulation of business logic within the database, promoting a uniform application of rules.
